'''Alexander Christison''' [[FRSE]] (1751–1820) was a [[Scottish people|Scottish]] educator, [[Professor of Classics (Edinburgh)|Professor of Humanity]] at the [[University of Edinburgh]], and mathematician during the [[Scottish Enlightenment]].

==Life==
He was born in 1753, at Redpath House, [[Longformacus]], [[Berwickshire]]. He was the eldest of seven children to a tenant sheep-farmer in the [[Lammermuir Hills]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.classicsandclass.info/product/204/|title=Classics & Class » Alexander Christison: The Lammermuir Latinist.|date=9 November 2015 }}</ref>

After a local education he began employment as the local schoolteacher for the parish of [[Edrom]] before attending the [[University of Edinburgh]] to study Classics, graduating in 1775. This background gave him access to teach at a higher calibre of school and he taught both at [[George Watson’s College]], [[Dalkeith Grammar School]] and the [[Royal High School, Edinburgh|High School in Edinburgh]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf |title=Archived copy |website=www.royalsoced.org.uk |access-date=14 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130124115814/http://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf |archive-date=24 January 2013 |url-status=dead}}</ref> In the 1780s he lived at Alexander's Land in the Bristo area.<ref>Edinburgh and Leith Post Office Directory 1784-1785</ref>

He was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] in 1800 his main proposer being the physician, [[James Gregory (physician)|James Gregory]]. He trained under [[John Hill (classicist)|John Hill]] at the [[University of Edinburgh]] and graduated MA in 1806, and from that date he served as professor of humanity at the university.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://collections.ed.ac.uk/art/record/535|title = "John Hill"}}</ref>

He died in Edinburgh on 25 June 1820 and is buried in [[Greyfriars Kirkyard]] in the city centre. He is buried in the plot of [[George Dunbar (classical scholar)|Professor George Dunbar]] at the north-west section of the western extension. He is also memorialised on [[Robert Christison]]'s grave at New Calton.

==Family==
Christison's son was Scottish toxicologist [[Robert Christison]] and Scottish minister (another) Alexander Chistison. His grandchildren included [[Sir Alexander Christison]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://archives.collections.ed.ac.uk/repositories/2/resources/86771|title=Papers of the Christison Family|work=Archives Online|publisher=University of Edinburgh|access-date=2024-05-10}}</ref> and the Australian explorer and pastoralist [[Robert Christison (pastoralist)|Robert Christison]].<ref>{{Citation|last=Allingham|first=E. M.|title=Christison, Robert (1837–1915)|url=https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/christison-robert-222|work=Australian Dictionary of Biography|place=Canberra|publisher=National Centre of Biography, Australian National University|language=en|access-date=2021-11-19}}</ref>

==Publications==
*''On the General Diffusion of Knowledge'' (1802) in which he said "genius is no respecter of ranks"
